profile.subject: NoSQL
profile.notes: FINAL QUIZ of this A-to-Z course: a practice check written for the course, not the professor's exam. The 20 minutes and the points are the quiz's own design, not facts about any exam.

questions.prompt: When does the course recommend keeping more replicas?
options: When data is easy to regenerate and reload
When you have little tolerance for data loss
When writes must be as fast as possible
When the cluster has a single server
questions.explanation: More replicas make data loss less likely, at a possible cost in performance. Fewer replicas suit data that is easy to regenerate and reload.
questions.quote: Use when you have little tolerance for data loss.

questions.prompt: In the Redis lab's manual failover, the command ____ turns replica 1 into the new master.
questions.explanation: Task 3.4 promotes replica 1 with REPLICAOF NO ONE, then attaches replica 2 to it. (SLAVEOF NO ONE is the older Redis spelling of the same command; it is not in the lab.)

questions.prompt: In the ring example, keys map to 0-95 across 8 servers. How many values does each server own?
questions.explanation: 96 values over 8 servers: each owns a range of 12 (S1 0-11, S2 12-23, and so on).
questions.quote: 8 servers each own a range of 12 values

questions.prompt: Which three properties does the CAP theorem say a distributed database cannot guarantee all at the same time?
questions.explanation: Consistency, availability and partition protection. Durability and isolation are ACID letters.
questions.quote: A distributed database cannot guarantee all three of these at the same time
questions.trap: Mixing the CAP letters with the ACID letters.

questions.prompt: A higher read quorum gives fresher data, at the cost of higher ____.
questions.explanation: L4#39: waiting for more matching answers means waiting for slower replicas.
questions.quote: A higher read quorum gives fresher data, at the cost of higher latency.

questions.prompt: Which strength of eventual consistency guarantees that reads only move forward in time?
questions.explanation: Monotonic read: once you have seen a value, you will never see an earlier version of it. Monotonic write is about the order of your writes.
questions.quote: reads only move forward in time
questions.trap: Confusing monotonic read with monotonic write.

questions.prompt: Task 3.5: on a masterless cluster, at 21:47:03 journalist A sends match:1001:homeGoals = 2 to node 1 while journalist B sends match:1001:homeGoals = 1 to node 3. Why can this conflict happen here but not on the Redis master-slave set-up, and what simple rule could decide which value wins?
questions.modelAnswer: In a masterless cluster every node accepts writes, so two nodes can accept different values for the same key: masterless replication must handle write conflicts between nodes. In Redis master-slave only the master accepts writes, so both journalists would write to the same place in some order. A simple rule: keep the highest value, because a goal count only rises during a match (last write wins would need a tie-breaker, since both writes carry the same second).
rubric: Masterless: any node accepts writes, so two nodes can hold different values
Master-slave: only the master accepts writes, so no conflict between nodes
Proposes one simple rule (for example highest value or last write wins)
Justifies the rule for this scenario (goals only rise, or the same-second tie)
questions.explanation: L4#10 says masterless must handle write conflicts between nodes; the course asks you to propose the rule and gives no official one.

questions.prompt: A report runs against 5 replicas and must read a consistent value, even if it is the slowest read. Which read threshold does the course give for that?
questions.explanation: With 5 replicas, threshold 5 guarantees a consistent read but is slowest. Threshold 1 is fastest but may be stale; 3 agrees by majority.
questions.quote: threshold 5 guarantees a consistent read but is slowest
questions.trap: Choosing 3: the slide calls it majority agreement, not a guaranteed consistent read.

questions.prompt: During the 90-second split of the ride-hailing exercise, the app favours CP. Which consequences follow from the course's definition of CP?
options: Every query still gets a response
questions.explanation: CP is consistent and partition-tolerant and blocks some queries, so availability suffers. Returning stale data is the AP behaviour, and a response to every query is availability.
questions.quote: Consistent + partition-tolerant, blocks some queries (availability suffers).

questions.prompt: A user updates her address on one server; a nearby replica updates instantly but a data center thousands of miles away lags. Which BASE property describes this, and which guarantee would make sure she herself never sees her old address after the update?
questions.modelAnswer: Eventually consistent: copies may differ briefly, then converge once replication catches up. To make sure she never sees her old address after writing the new one, the system needs read-your-writes consistency (or session consistency, if it is enough within her current session).
rubric: Names eventual consistency (the E of BASE)
Copies differ briefly, then converge once replication catches up
Mentions session consistency as the one-session variant
questions.explanation: L3#11 gives the address example; L3#12 defines read-your-writes and session consistency.
questions.quote: a data center thousands of miles away lags
